assignment: Your principal has decided that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. For example, students could participate in sports, work on the yearbook, or serve on the student council. Do you agree or disagree with this decision? Use specific details and examples to convince others to support your position.
essay_1:
I agree with my principal's decision that every student should have to do at least one extracurricular activity. School is not just about passing tests. A lot of the real learning happens after the last bell, and you can't get it from a classroom.

My first reason is that activities help students build skills they will actually use. Like if you are on yearbook, you have to meet deadlines, take pictures, write captions, and work with the other editors. If one person is late, the whole book is late. You can't learn that from a worksheet. Student council is the same. They have to plan a fall dance, make a budget, and argue about whether to spend the money on a DJ or decorations. Adults do the same stuff at their jobs every day.

My second reason is that activities help students feel like they belong. Lots of kids feel lost at a big school, especially when they are new. When I started here I didn't know anybody and I ate lunch by myself for weeks. Then a friend talked me into joining cross-country. After about a month I had people to sit with and I actually looked forward to practice. Kids who feel connected to their school come more often and care more about their grades. If the activity is required, every student gets that chance, even the shy ones who would never sign up on their own.

Some people say a requirement isn't fair because some students have jobs or have to watch their little brothers and sisters. That is a good point, but we can fix it without getting rid of the rule. The school could have activities during lunch or have short meetings, and it could count community service or clubs outside of school. The rule can be flexible but it should still be there. If it isn't, the students who need a place to belong the most will probably be the ones who stay away.

Other people say students already have too much homework. But I think kids who stay active manage their time better, not worse. When you have a busy schedule you have to plan. Lots of athletes and band members get their homework done faster because they know practice is coming up. I know this because on days I have practice I do my homework right after school, and I never waste time.

In conclusion, requiring one activity is a small thing to ask for a big reward. It makes students try something new, meet new people, and practice teamwork and responsibility. For these reasons I support the principal's decision, and I think our school will be a better place because of it.
essay_2:
I agree with the principal that every student should join at least one extracurricular activity. School is about more than passing tests, and the time after the last bell is when students learn things a classroom can teach only a little.

First, activities help students build skills. A student on the yearbook has to meet deadlines, take photos, and work with a team of editors. If one person is late, the whole book is late, and that is a problem. A student in the band learns to show up on time and practice a part until it fits with the others. Student council is another example. They plan the fall dance, set a budget, and argue about whether to spend money on a DJ or on decorations. Adults use these skills at work every day, so it makes sense to practice early.

Second, activities give students a place to belong. Lots of kids feel lost at a big school, especially in ninth grade. When I was new, I knew nobody, and I sat alone at lunch for weeks. Then a friend talked me into joining the cross-country team. Within a month I had friends to sit with, and I liked going to practice. Students who feel connected at school come more often and care more about their grades. A required activity gives every student that chance, even the shy ones who would stay home instead of signing up.

Some people say a requirement is unfair because certain students have jobs or have to watch their little brothers and sisters. That is a fair worry, but we can handle it without losing the rule. The school can offer clubs during lunch or short sessions, and it can count community service done outside school. Students could pick a club by interest, like chess, art, or robotics. The rule should be flexible, but it should stay. Without it, the students who need friends the most are the ones who stay away.

Others say students have too much homework already. However, I think busy students often manage their time better. A full schedule forces a person to plan. Many athletes and band members finish homework faster because practice is coming. I have seen this on my own team, where the fastest runners are often on the honor roll.

In the end, one required activity is a small ask. It pushes students to try new things, meet people, and practice teamwork. For these reasons, I support the principal's decision, even though some students will complain at first, and the school will be a different place with it.
